body:
From fibre to fabric

A textile is a material made from fibres or yarns. Traditional Indian textile production includes spinning, weaving, dyeing, printing, embroidery and several other forms of ornamentation.

Common natural textile fibres include:

  • Cotton: a plant fibre that is cleaned, spun into yarn and woven into fabric.
  • Silk: a protein fibre obtained from silkworm cocoons and valued for its lustre.
  • Wool: an animal fibre valued especially for warmth and used in shawls, blankets and other textiles.

A fibre becomes yarn through spinning or another suitable yarn-making process. The yarn is then arranged or combined to produce fabric. Different fibres, yarn qualities and weaving arrangements produce different textures and uses.

Warp, weft and the handloom

In ordinary woven fabric, 2 sets of yarns cross each other.

  • Warp: the yarns arranged lengthwise on the loom.
  • Weft: the yarns passed across the warp to form the fabric.

A loom is the equipment used to interlace these yarns. A handloom is operated through human effort rather than the powered weaving mechanism characteristic of a powerloom.

The term handloom concerns the way the fabric is woven. It does not automatically tell us whether the yarn was spun by hand, whether the dyes are natural or whether the finished cloth is embroidered.

Handloom, powerloom and khadi are different terms

Handloom fabric is woven on a manually operated loom. It can use yarn produced by hand or by a spinning mill.

Powerloom fabric is woven on a loom whose weaving operations are driven by power.

Khadi is distinguished by its hand-spun yarn and hand-woven fabric. It became particularly important during the Indian national movement because Mahatma Gandhi promoted spinning and khadi as expressions of self-reliance, village employment and resistance to dependence on imported cloth.

All khadi involves hand weaving, but every handloom fabric is not necessarily khadi. A handloom saree woven from mill-spun silk yarn does not become khadi merely because the loom was operated by hand.

When is the design created?

One of the most useful ways to classify Indian textile crafts is to identify the stage at which the design is produced.

StageWhat happens?Examples
Before weavingYarns are coloured or otherwise prepared in advance to create the intended design.Ikat, including Patola
During weavingThe fabric structure or additional yarns create the pattern on the loom.Brocade, Tangaliya
After weavingThe completed cloth is coloured or decorated.Bandhani, block printing, embroidery

This classification concerns the principal stage of ornamentation. A finished textile may combine several stages. For example, a woven cloth can subsequently receive Bandhani dots or embroidery.

Ikat: patterning the yarn before weaving

Ikat uses resist-dyed yarns. Selected parts of the yarn are protected before dyeing so that colours form a predetermined pattern when the yarns are woven.

In single ikat, 1 set of yarns, generally either warp or weft, carries the resist-dyed pattern. In double ikat, both warp and weft yarns are patterned and must be aligned during weaving.

Patan Patola is a celebrated example of double ikat.

Tie-dye on finished fabric

Bandhani generally involves tying small portions of an already woven fabric before dyeing it. The tied portions resist the dye and produce dots or other patterns when the ties are removed.

Both ikat and Bandhani use resist-dye principles, but they differ in what is tied and when the pattern is created. Ikat patterns the yarn before weaving; Bandhani patterns the fabric.

Block printing and embroidery

Block printing transfers a design to cloth using carved blocks. Depending on the tradition, dye or a resist substance may be applied through successive impressions.

Embroidery uses needlework or related stitching methods to decorate an existing textile. Mirrors, beads and other ornaments may also be attached.

Appliqué involves attaching pieces of fabric to a base fabric to create a decorative composition.

A cloth can therefore be handwoven without being embroidered, embroidered without being handwoven, or both handwoven and embroidered.

Why materials and methods should not be confused

Some familiar textile terms describe a material, others describe a method, and still others identify a regional product.

  • Silk describes a fibre.
  • Handloom describes a way of weaving.
  • Ikat describes a method of patterning yarns.
  • Bandhani describes a resist-dye method applied to fabric.
  • Patan Patola identifies a particular regional textile tradition.
  • Zari describes metallic decorative thread used in textiles.

Prelims focus

  • Warp: lengthwise yarns; weft: crosswise yarns.
  • Handloom: manually operated weaving equipment.
  • Khadi: hand-spun and hand-woven textile.
  • Ikat: yarn is resist-dyed before weaving.
  • Double ikat: both warp and weft are patterned before weaving.
  • Bandhani: resist-dye patterning of woven fabric.
  • Trap: Handloom, khadi, embroidery and Bandhani describe different characteristics and are not interchangeable terms.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Textiles', printed pp. 83–96, especially 'Yarn, Threads and Fibres' and 'Textile Techniques'; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class XII, 'Mahatma Gandhi and Self-sufficiency', printed pp. 31–34; India Handloom Brand, Ministry of Textiles, 'Gujarat Single Ikat Saree', sections 'Material used' and 'Technique used', accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: Handloom and Textile Crafts: Fibres, Weaving and Decoration

body:
Patan Patola: the double-ikat silk tradition

Patan Patola is a celebrated silk textile associated with Patan in Gujarat. The traditional weaving heritage is closely associated with Salvi weaver families.

Its defining characteristic is double ikat. Both the warp and the weft yarns are tied and dyed according to a planned design before weaving begins. During weaving, the coloured portions must come together to form the intended pattern.

This distinguishes Patola from a printed saree, where colour is applied to the surface of a previously woven cloth.

Traditional Patola designs include geometrical arrangements and stylised motifs such as elephants, birds, flowers and other ornamental forms. Patola textiles have also formed part of ceremonial clothing and wedding traditions.

Because the design is produced through the arrangement of coloured yarns, a woven ikat pattern can be visible on both faces of the cloth. However, reversibility by itself does not prove that a fabric is double ikat; some single-ikat fabrics are also reversible.

Patan Patola and Rajkot Patola

Rajkot Patola is a separate regional textile tradition, with its own geographical indication. Gujarat's single-ikat sarees are particularly associated with weaving centres in Rajkot and Surendranagar.

In single weft ikat, the weft yarns are patterned before weaving, while the other yarn set generally provides the background structure. Such textiles can produce complex designs at a lower production cost than elaborate Patan double ikat.

The usual comparison is useful, but it must be stated correctly: Patan is especially renowned for double ikat, while Rajkot is strongly associated with single ikat; both single- and double-ikat textiles are produced in the wider Rajkot and Surendranagar weaving region.

Bandhani: tie-dye patterns on fabric

Bandhani is a resist-dye tradition in which small portions of fabric are tied to prevent dye from reaching them. When the cloth is dyed and the ties are opened, the protected areas form contrasting patterns.

Jamnagar and Kutch are important Bandhani centres in Gujarat. The method is also practised in Rajasthan.

Traditional Bandhani appears in sarees, odhanis, turbans and ceremonial garments. Its dots and patterned arrangements may be associated with weddings, festivals and community customs.

The essential distinction from ikat is that Bandhani works on the woven cloth, whereas ikat patterns the yarn before weaving.

Ajrakh: resist and block-printed textiles of Kutch

Ajrakh is a traditional textile-printing practice associated with Kutch and the wider historical Sindh-Kutch region. Gujarat's well-known centres include Ajrakhpur and Dhamadka.

Ajrakh uses carefully planned block-printed and resist-dyed patterns. Traditional designs frequently feature geometrical arrangements, with colours such as indigo blue, red and black.

A principal feature of Ajrakh is the interaction between repeated block impressions and successive colouring or resist processes. Ajrakh is therefore classified with printed and dyed textiles, not with embroidered fabrics or ikat weaving.

The craft also illustrates regional transmission: related printing traditions developed across Kutch and Sindh, while individual production centres acquired their own characteristics.

Gharchola: a ceremonial Gujarati textile

Gharchola is a traditional Gujarati ceremonial textile closely associated with marriage customs.

It commonly combines a characteristic checked or grid arrangement, often formed with zari, with Bandhani-style tied and dyed motifs within the squares. Red and related auspicious colours are prominent in many traditional examples.

Gharchola should not be confused with Patola. Patola is identified especially by ikat weaving, whereas Gharchola is identified by its characteristic grid, tie-dye decoration and marriage-related use.

Mashru: a silk-cotton textile tradition

Mashru is another important textile associated with Gujarat. It traditionally combines silk and cotton in a woven fabric, producing a lustrous appearance.

Mashru demonstrates why a textile must sometimes be identified by its fibre combination and weave rather than by the presence of printed, tied or embroidered decoration.

Surat and the zari tradition

Zari is metallic thread or metallic-looking decorative yarn used in textiles. Surat is a major historic centre associated with zari production and trade.

Zari may be incorporated into woven brocades and ceremonial fabrics or used in embroidery. Thus, zari describes the decorative material, while brocade weaving and embroidery describe different ways of applying it.

Comparing Gujarat's major textile forms

FormMain identificationImportant centre
Patan PatolaDouble-ikat silk weavingPatan
Rajkot PatolaRegional ikat weaving; especially associated with single ikatRajkot
BandhaniTied and dyed fabricJamnagar and Kutch
AjrakhBlock-printed and resist-dyed geometrical patternsKutch
GharcholaGrid pattern, zari and tie-dye; wedding associationGujarat
MashruLustrous silk-cotton woven fabricGujarat
Surat ZariMetallic decorative thread and associated craftSurat

Prelims focus

  • Patan Patola: Patan; Salvi weaving tradition; double ikat.
  • Rajkot Patola: separately recognised regional ikat tradition.
  • Jamnagar and Kutch: important Bandhani centres.
  • Ajrakh: Kutch; block printing and resist dyeing.
  • Gharchola: checked zari pattern, Bandhani decoration and marriage customs.
  • Mashru: silk-cotton woven textile.
  • Trap: Both ikat and Bandhani involve resist dyeing, but ikat patterns yarns before weaving and Bandhani patterns woven cloth.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Crafts Heritage', printed p. 9, and 'Textiles', printed pp. 83–96; India Handloom Brand, Ministry of Textiles, 'Gujarat Single Ikat Saree', sections 'Background', 'Technique used' and 'How to distinguish genuine Gujarat Single Ikat Saree', accessed 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, GI application details for Patan Patola, application 232, and Kutch Ajrakh Print of Gujarat, application 1050; Intellectual Property India, state-wise registered GI list, applications 221, 232, 380, 756, 838 and 1050, data as of 31 December 2025; Gujarat Tourism, 'Handicrafts' and 'Niche Tourism', Gujarat textile listings, accessed 23 November 2026.]
